text: Question three. How do you review code an assistant wrote? Like a pull request from a capable stranger. Check that it does what was asked, and nothing else. That every import, function and parameter it uses exists. That it handles the boundaries and the error paths. That it doesn't add an accidental O of n squared loop, or an N plus one query, one database call per row. And that its tests would fail without the change. Then run it. Go back to the diff as it arrived, before it shipped. It touches one function and its tests, and nothing else. It calls nothing that doesn't exist. It makes one pass over the input. So far, so good. The boundaries are where it breaks. Besides the missing sort, the comparison is a strict less-than. These are closed intervals, so one to two and two to three share the point two, and should merge. The code keeps them apart. And a merge sets the end to the new interval's end, even when that's smaller. One to ten, then two to three, becomes one to three. The merge shrank the interval it should have kept. Last check: its tests. Would they fail if the code were wrong? The first passes on this code and on a correct version alike, so it can't tell them apart. The second asserts that one to two and two to three stay apart. That's the bug, written down as a requirement, and on correct code it fails. Three changes fix it: sort the input, compare with less-than-or-equal, and keep the larger end. Then write the tests the review wanted: unsorted, touching and contained. On the assistant's code, all three fail, which is what failing without the change looks like. On the fix, all three pass. Each bug is a boundary or an unstated assumption, which is where to look first. The obvious test touched none of them. Then expect the follow-up: should touching intervals merge at all? Half-open booking slots, nine to ten and ten to eleven, don't overlap. So ask whether the end is inclusive, and write the answer down as a test. The fix also added a sort, which takes the merge from one pass to n log n. Reading code includes judging what it costs. Next: algorithms as reasoning.
